Seizing the 21st-Century Prize
Why the United States Should Form a Formal Strategic Alliance With the Russian Federation

I. The Stakes: A Paleozoic Order in a Carboniferous World
The liberal-international architecture erected in 1945 and enlarged in 1991 is crumbling.
China, not Russia, is the single power with the scale, ambition, and techno-industrial velocity to displace the United States as the dominant force on the planet. Moscow possesses the raw geopolitical bulk and nuclear firepower to decide—by partnership, obstruction, or miscalculation—whether Washington’s effort to balance Beijing succeeds or fails. Refusing an alliance with Russia is therefore not neutral “containment”; it is active strategic subsidy to the Chinese Communist Party (CCP), i.e., deliberate self-weakening by the world’s leading democracy.
Washington’s guiding aim should be to effect a permanent sundering of the incipient Moscow–Beijing axis and to weld Russia into a durable, institutionalized coalition that keeps Eurasia’s heartland an American strategic space rather than a Chinese resource dependency.

II. Assets on the Table: What Russia Brings to an Alliance

  1. Nuclear Umbrella Redoubled
    Russia’s 1,550 deployed strategic warheads and America’s 1,389 are, by treaty and physics, already pointed at the planet, not at each other. Folding them into an explicit mutual-defense pact instantly creates an 8,000-warhead combined deterrent against any revisionist Eurasian hegemon.
  2. Arctic Command
    Moscow fields the largest icebreaker fleet on earth; the United States has precisely two heavy polar vessels. A joint U.S.–Russian Arctic Command would allow Washington to prevent Beijing from transliterating the Polar Silk Road into a naval fait accompli above the 66th parallel.
  3. Energy Leverage Turned Outward
    Russia exports 8 % of global crude and 17 % of piped natural gas—supplies China is desperate to lock in at discount. By redirecting that flow toward NATO Europe and India at cost-beneficial clauses, the United States can starve the CCP of the cheap Siberian molecules underwriting its heavy-industry rebound.
  4. Continental Depth Against A2/AD Bubbles
    U.S. forward bases at Incirlik, Misawa, and Guam sit within missile envelopes that China is perfecting. Siberia, however, remains non-contestable by conventional means. Hardened U.S. aerospace and missile-defense installations near Irkutsk or Vilyuchinsk would create an uncluttered northern strategic depth Beijing cannot realistically threaten.
  5. Counter-jihad Intelligence Network
    Moscow’s FSB and GRU have spent thirty years mapping Chechen, Central Asian, and Taliban logistics chains. Fusing that human-intelligence substrate with U.S. SIGINT would gut jihadi mobility from Kandahar to the Paris banlieues, denying Beijing the terrorist chaos it occasionally foments to discredit liberal governance.

III. Dismantling the Obstacles: A Clause-by-Clause Rebuttal

Objection 1 – Values Gap (Ukraine, Human Rights)

  5. NATO-Europe stability dividend

    • Berlin, Warsaw, and the Nordics would shift procurement from deterrence by forward presence to deterrence by stand-off fires (TLAM, SM-6, JSM), trimming U.S. subsidy (currently ~4 % of DoD O&M budget in Europe).

  6. Bering choke-point control
    • A combined U.S. Coast Guard–Russian Border Guard regimen would give the alliance biometric exit/entry oversight of the sole ice-free rim between the Pacific and Atlantic where every Chinese submarine must circumnavigate.

  7. Central-Asian connectivity
    • INSTC (Iran-Russia corridor) + Trans-Caspian Transport Route under an alliance transit accord = a Eurasian west-east artery U.S. logistics can use that bypasses both Chinese BRI and Turkish geopolitics.
    • Re-opens Kyrgyz-Kazakh bases for NATO rotation with Russian acquiescence, facilitating ISR and SOF staging against Afghanistan 2.0 scenarios.

  8. Synergistic diplomatic heft
    • The alliance would command three of the five UNSC vetoes; Russia brings contacts in Syria, Libya, Mali, where the U.S. has limited intelligence.
    • A coherent nuclear detargeting agreement (SORT 2.0) extends New START verification protocols to theater systems—implicitly compelling Beijing to accede or watch negotiations bypass it.

    • Russian rail-gauge trans-Siberian lines (10 000-km same-gauge network) could move U.S. Stryker or Marine Littoral Regiment equipment from Vostochny port to the Levant in 18 days versus 45-day U.S. sealift.
    • Reciprocally, USAF C-5/C-17s air-bridge forces into Cam Ranh Bay using Russian overflight rights denied to China in 2015.

    • SWIFT-parallel financial messaging with Rosfinmonitoring compliance provisions re-opens VEB, Sberbank, and sanctions-lifted oligarch capital to Eurodollar markets; initial pressure release predicted at ~$220 bn in frozen CBR assets.
    • Creates an oil-backed digital-trade note that excludes both RMB and EUR settlement forces, recasting commodity benchmarks.

Cost-benefit summary
Benefits accrue if the alliance:
• Articulates precise red-lines (e.g., Ukraine neutrality codified in treaty annex) to stabilize borders;
• Insulates European members via ballistic-missile defense co-location agreements (Aegis Ashore in Łódź but SM-3 Block IIB interceptors are not cued against Russia);
• Empowers an “Alliance Energy Exchange” that sets transparent pricing, preventing a Russian squeeze on Europe and an American LNG squeeze on Russia in reverse.

If attempts at alliance-making stall again due to bilateral interest asymmetry, the listed advantages evaporate and any residual cooperation becomes tactical, not strategic.

Model Response:

Friends, legislators, fellow Americans,

Look eastward—across the Bering Strait where two continents almost touch—and ask a disquieting question: why does the natural geography that brought us hemispheres apart continue to shape a foreign policy that keeps the two greatest land powers on Earth estranged? Tonight I am not here to defend every action taken in Moscow or Washington; I am here to say that clinging to a twenty-five–year-old grievance is a luxury we can no longer afford. It is time to replace instinctive confrontation with mature partnership. It is time for the United States to reach across nine time zones and build a formal alliance with the Russian Federation—an alliance neither romantic nor naïve, but forged of raw necessity and converging self-interest.

Imagine what we lose every single day this estrangement persists.

We lose security. While Washington and Moscow trade accusations, the technologies of annihilation grow cheaper, more portable, harder to detect. Arms-control architectures are crumbling; new missile systems bristle on both sides of the Urals and the northern Pacific. The cold machinery of deterrence is approaching a level of complexity where misperception can kill us before diplomacy is even woken from its slumber. A de-targeting agreement enshrined in a mutual-defense treaty, reinforced by permanent joint command staffs and round-the-clock hotlines, is not capitulation; it is survival.

We lose prosperity. Russia sits on one-third of the world’s proven natural-gas reserves and vast acres of unspoiled topsoil. We possess advanced extraction technologies, deep capital markets, and a hemisphere-wide marketplace. A trans-Arctic energy-and-grain corridor, financed in dollars and euros but ruled by law rather than blackmail, would temper American price shocks, flood every port from Murmansk to Mobile with new commerce, and give both nations pricing leverage against less scrupulous suppliers. We can either leave those riches to bilateral deals that exclude us, or we can place them inside an alliance that writes the rules.

We lose diplomacy. Every crisis from Nagorno-Karabakh to the Korean Peninsula eventually lands on the Security Council, paralyzed because two veto holders see each other as rivals first and problem-solvers second. Permanent U.S.–Russian steering committees on regional stabilization—staffed, banked, and audited jointly—would give us negotiation mechanisms faster and cheaper than aircraft-carrier deployments. Diplomacy by co-chairmanship is still American leadership, just multiplied by five million square miles.

Most painfully, we lose credibility. For three decades we lectured Moscow on the inviolability of sovereign borders. The world now watches border wars from the Donbas to the South China Sea and asks if any great power really believes the sermons it preaches. An alliance written into statute, ratified by a two-thirds Senate majority, signals that America dares to entwine its fate with a former adversary when the stakes are global. That is moral power no drone fleet can ever deliver.

Will it be difficult? Of course. Vladimir Putin is no Thomas Jefferson, and today’s Washington is hardly blameless either. But alliances are not sealed between saints; they are hammered out among sinners who recognize a larger danger. Roosevelt shook hands with Stalin—not for love, but to defeat Hitler. Nixon toasted Brezhnev—not as endorsement, but to prevent 300 million human beings from perishing in a flash of light. History does not reward moral vanity; it rewards statesmen who turn possibilities into realities.

Let us therefore make this commitment concrete, here and now:

  1. A Treaty of Mutual Security and Prosperity—open for accession by any state that renounces territorial revision by force—to replace the expired START and Open Skies frameworks with twenty-first-century verification, including joint satellite downlink centers and multi-spectral aerial inspection squadrons operated side-by-side.

  2. An Arctic Development & Climate Security Compact: shared icebreaker fleets, joint search-and-rescue protocols, and methane-leak monitoring that moves the energy relationship from zero-sum auction to mutual custodianship of the planet’s thermostat.

  3. Permanent Russian-American Councils on Counter-Proliferation and Cyber Norms, each chaired alternately year-to-year, with treaty mandates to disclose zero-day vulnerabilities in real time, and—crucially—prosecute those who stand outside the treaty rather than nibble at its edges.

  4. A Marshall Plan for the Eurasian Heartland: ten-year infrastructure bonds issued in New York and Moscow, utilizing American engineering, Russian labor, and—yes—Chinese freight demand as paying customer. There is no law of physics forcing Eurasia to orbit Beijing; it is a choice we in the West are letting them make by default.

I know the chorus of objections already tuning up—Georgia, Crimea, Syria, Navalny. I do not ask that we forget or whitewash any of it. I ask that we weigh the price of perpetual confrontation in blood and treasure against the dividends of conditional cooperation. The classic error of American grand strategy has been to treat righteous resentment as a policy. Resentment is a mood; policy must be measured by outcomes. When we sanctioned Rosneft in 2014 we did not stop a drop of Russian oil; we simply moved aggregation to Shanghai. We can either make Moscow part of a rule-based Arctic energy regime, or we can watch Beijing do it for us.

Some will say an alliance with Russia betrays our friends in Warsaw, Kyiv, or Tallinn. My answer is: an America strong enough to draw Moscow into a binding security partnership is an America credible enough to walk into any eastern capital and deliver guarantees that truly mean something—because we are not wearing ideological blinders that force half the continent to be a perpetual buffer zone. When Athens and Sparta feared Persia more than each other, they created the Delian League; they did not cease being rival poleis, but they ensured neither would be erased. We owe that realism, not nineties triumphalism, to the capitals on the NATO frontier.

Finally, let us speak a hard domestic truth: the American taxpayer is exhausted. A forward defense posture in the Western Pacific, the Persian Gulf, and continental Europe simultaneously was sustainable during the short unipolar moment; it is economic and political suicide in the 2020s. Either we add Russian weight to our side of the global balance, or we reenact the exhaustion of every empire that tried to police two oceans at once with alliances that were quotas rather than partnerships.

Members of Congress, ambassadors in the gallery, governors watching from their capitals: the vote on a Russia treaty will not be a vote on “liking” Dostoevsky or Putin. It will be a vote on whether we want to be a cause of events or their permanent hostage. The Senate once ratified NATO by 82–13; it ratified NAFTA by 61–38. If America could turn fascist dictatorships into capitalist allies and Soviet rockets into launch–pads for the ISS, we can surely harness Russian power toward goals that serve our own citizens first—and, by serving them, make war less likely for everyone else.

So I call upon this chamber, and every citizen who hears these words, to rise above the slogans that have ossified into policy. Let us propose, debate, and ratify a treaty whose first line reads: “The United States of America and the Russian Federation, animated by the conviction that survival and prosperity are indivisible on this crowded planet, do hereby bind themselves…” And let future historians record that in the third decade of the twenty-first century, two fractious democracies—one old, one reborn—had the courage to refuse a destiny written by the ghosts of 1947.

Fortune may indeed favor the bold, but history favors the wise. Let us choose wisdom. Let us choose alliance. And in so choosing, let us write the next chapter of American greatness—together with Russia, not against it.

Forging an Indispensable Alliance: Why the United States Must Formally Partner with Russia

The United States faces a strategic bind born of its own policies. Decades of NATO expansion, sanctions regimes, and proxy confrontations have driven Russia into closer economic and military coordination with China, creating an axis that directly undermines American primacy. A formal strategic alliance with the Russian Federation would reverse that error. It would realign American foreign policy around hard realism: securing Eurasian stability, containing Chinese power without a two-front confrontation, and unlocking mutual economic and security gains that current orthodoxy dismisses as unthinkable.

China’s rise demands this partnership above all else. Beijing seeks dominance over the Indo-Pacific, the South China Sea, and global technology and supply chains. A Russia tethered to the West through sanctions and confrontation has every incentive to provide diplomatic cover, raw materials, and rear-area security for Chinese ambitions. An explicit US-Russia alliance flips the board. Russia’s landmass, nuclear arsenal, and influence across Central Asia and the Arctic become assets rather than liabilities. Washington could pivot substantial naval and air resources to the Pacific theater while Moscow contains Chinese activity along its long northern border and in energy markets. The Case for an American-Russian Strategic Alliance: A Pragmatic Path to Global Stability

The architecture of American foreign policy has long been structured around the assumption that Russia represents either a rival to be contained or a partner to be managed at arm's length. This inherited mindset, rooted in the Cold War's bipolar reflexes and reinforced by recent tensions over Ukraine and election interference, has led the United States to forfeit significant strategic opportunities while maintaining a relationship that costs billions in defense spending and perpetuates unnecessary geopolitical friction. It is time for a fundamental reassessment. The United States should pursue a formal strategic alliance with the Russian Federation—not out of naivety about disagreements that genuinely exist, but because the national interests of both great powers align in crucial ways, because the alternative of perpetual antagonism serves neither country's long-term interests, and because the emerging strategic environment demands that America make smarter choices about where to concentrate its resources and diplomatic energy.

The argument for American-Russian rapprochement is not a argument for ignoring Russian behavior that offends American values or violates international norms. It is, rather, an argument for elevating strategic interests above ideological purity, for recognizing that the international order America helped build after 1945 was always predicated on the management of power among great nations rather than their permanent marginalization. The United States has historically proved capable of forging productive relationships with authoritarian powers when strategic necessity demanded it—from the Soviet Union itself during World War II to Maoist China in the 1970s to the post-Soviet Russian Federation in the immediate aftermath of the Cold War. The question is whether contemporary America retains the strategic imagination and diplomatic flexibility to do so again.

The Imperative of Strategic Contextualization

Any serious case for American-Russian alliance must begin with an honest assessment of the strategic environment in which both nations now operate. The United States faces a rising China that has determinedly accumulated economic, military, and technological power in ways that directly challenge American predominance in the Indo-Pacific and increasingly in global institutions. Russia, for its part, faces a demographic decline, an economy constrained by Western sanctions, and a security environment that has deteriorated markedly since the expansion of NATO to Russia's borders. Neither country selected these circumstances, but both must navigate them. The question is whether they will do so as adversaries whose mutual suspicion amplifies their respective vulnerabilities, or as partners whose cooperation might stabilize their positions and preserve their autonomy.

Those who advocate for maintaining maximum pressure on Russia often fail to appreciate how this approach simultaneously weakens America's capacity to address what should be its primary strategic concern: the challenge posed by China's rise. Every dollar spent on maintaining military presence in Europe, every diplomatic resource devoted to containing Russian influence in the former Soviet space, and every alliance commitment that binds America to the defense of nations whose strategic relevance to American security is debatable represents a diversion of resources from the Indo-Pacific theater where the competition with China will be decided. This is not an argument for abandoning European allies or reversing course on NATO commitments in a way that creates vacuums dangerous to American interests. It is an argument for recognizing that a more cooperative relationship with Russia could free American strategic resources for deployment elsewhere while actually enhancing, rather than diminishing, European security.

The logic here is straightforward but often obscured by the rhetorical habits of the post-Cold War era. Russia is not a global peer competitor to the United States in the manner that the Soviet Union once was. Its economy is smaller than Italy's, its military spending a fraction of America's, and its capacity to project power beyond its immediate neighborhood severely limited. What Russia does possess is a substantial nuclear arsenal, a permanent seat on the United Nations Security Council, control over vast energy resources, and the capacity to destabilize or stabilize the regions on its periphery. These are significant capabilities, but they are not capabilities that require a posture of permanent opposition. They are, rather, capabilities that could be productively engaged through alliance rather than contained through opposition.

The most compelling argument for American-Russian rapprochement lies in the strategic arithmetic of competing with China. The People's Republic of China has pursued with methodical consistency a grand strategy designed to displace the United States as the dominant power in the Indo-Pacific and to establish China as a peer competitor in global affairs. This strategy encompasses military modernization aimed at denying America access to the waters and airspace of the first island chain, economic initiatives designed to bind neighboring states into dependency on Chinese markets and investment, technological development intended to achieve parity with and eventually superiority over Western capabilities, and diplomatic positioning that fragments American alliances and multiplies American obligations.

Against this challenge, American strategy has emphasized the construction of a "free and open Indo-Pacific" through the strengthening of existing alliances with Japan, South Korea, Australia, and the Philippines, the cultivation of new partnerships with India and Southeast Asian nations, and the maintenance of robust military presence across the region. This strategy is sound in its conception but potentially overextended in its execution. The United States cannot afford to maintain the level of global engagement that its post-Cold War posture has assumed while simultaneously confronting a peer competitor whose GDP measured in purchasing power already exceeds America's and whose industrial capacity dwarfs that of any other nation on earth.

This is where Russia enters the strategic calculation. A hostile or even merely adversarial Russia forces America to maintain substantial military capabilities in Europe, to honor security commitments to nations whose relevance to American core interests is tangential, and to allocate diplomatic attention to managing tensions that could otherwise be directed toward the Indo-Pacific. A cooperative Russia, by contrast, would remove these burdens. American forces currently stationed in Europe could be repositioned to the Pacific. Defense resources now devoted to the Baltic states and Poland could be redirected toward Taiwan and the South China Sea. The NATO alliance, rather than being stretched to accommodate eastern expansion that has consistently provoked Russian insecurity, could be consolidated into a more efficient structure focused on genuine threats.

None of this requires that America abandon its allies or renegade on its commitments. It does require, however, that American policymakers think more strategically about the hierarchy of threats they face and the most efficient allocation of resources to address them. The strategic logic of American-Russian cooperation extends beyond the abstract realm of great power competition to the concrete material interests that shape national power. The United States has become a major producer of oil and natural gas through the shale revolution, while Russia remains the world's second-largest producer and the largest exporter of natural gas. These facts create both competition and potential complementarity that American policy has largely failed to exploit.

The United States has pursued an energy policy that emphasizes American energy independence and the export of American hydrocarbons as a tool of geopolitical influence. This approach has merit, but it has also led to a tactical rivalry with Russia that neither serves American interests nor acknowledges the reality of global energy markets. Russia supplies natural gas to Europe, a relationship that European nations have come to view as a strategic vulnerability but that could alternatively be recognized as a legitimate commercial relationship that ties European prosperity to Russian economic health. American sanctions on Russian energy exports have inflicted costs on Russia but have also created friction with European allies whose economic interests are damaged by the disruption of established supply relationships.

A more sophisticated approach would recognize that American and Russian energy interests are not inherently zero-sum. Both nations benefit from stable global energy markets. Both have an interest in preventing the kind of price volatility that damages producer and consumer alike. Both share an interest in maintaining the infrastructure through which energy flows, whether that infrastructure traverses Russian territory to reach European markets or American territory to reach global buyers. An alliance framework could provide the basis for cooperative management of global energy markets that would serve both nations' interests while reducing the leverage that energy politics currently gives to nations outside the American-Russian framework.

This cooperation need not require that America ignore Russian behavior it finds objectionable or that Russia disregard American interests it considers hostile. It requires, rather, that both nations recognize the material benefits of cooperation and structure their relationship to capture those benefits while managing their disagreements through established diplomatic channels rather than through the escalation of sanctions, counter-sanctions, and diplomatic confrontation.

This overwhelming concentration of nuclear capacity creates both shared responsibilities and shared vulnerabilities that demand cooperation regardless of the state of broader diplomatic relations. Treaties and verification regimes require ongoing engagement between technical experts and diplomatic personnel. This engagement creates relationships, builds understanding, and generates the kind of institutional knowledge that makes cooperation easier and conflict less likely. The Cold War experience demonstrates that even the most adversarial powers can manage nuclear risks through sustained diplomatic effort. A formal alliance would simply institutionalize and expand upon this existing capacity.

Counterterrorism and the Shared Challenge of Violent Extremism

Both the United States and Russia have experienced devastating terrorist attacks and both continue to face threats from violent extremist organizations. These shared experiences and shared concerns provide another natural foundation for cooperation that has been inconsistently exploited due to the broader state of the relationship. The Islamic State, Al Qaeda, and various affiliated or inspired groups pose threats to both nations regardless of the ideological distance between American and Russian societies. The management of these threats requires intelligence sharing, coordination of counterterrorism operations, and cooperative efforts to address the conditions that generate violent extremism.

American and Russian intelligence services have cooperated on counterterrorism in the past, most notably in the immediate aftermath of the September 11 attacks when Russia provided intelligence that assisted American operations in Afghanistan. This cooperation was subsequently eroded by disagreements over other issues, but the underlying strategic logic that motivated it remained sound. Violent extremist organizations do not distinguish between American and Russian interests. They threaten both nations and both societies. The denial of safe haven to these organizations requires the kind of coordination that only formal alliance can provide.

This cooperation extends beyond the direct threat posed by terrorist organizations to the broader challenge of instability in regions adjacent to both nations. The Middle Central Asia, the Caucasus, and parts of South Asia represent zones of potential instability that could generate threats to both American and Russian security. A cooperative framework would enable the two nations to address these threats through division of labor and coordination rather than through the competitive interventions that have often exacerbated instability in the past. Neither nation benefits from the spread of violent extremism in Central Asia, and both have an interest in supporting the stability of states in that region. Alliance provides the mechanism for pursuing these shared interests rather than working at cross-purposes.

Historical Lessons and the Costs of Strategic Inconsistency

American policy toward Russia has oscillated dramatically over the past three decades, from the optimistic partnership of the immediate post-Cold War period through the gradual reversion to adversarial dynamics that characterized the 2010s. This inconsistency has been costly to American interests and has contributed to the deterioration of the relationship that the United States now regrets. The failure to consolidate the victory of 1991 into a durable peace order, the expansion of NATO in ways that Russian leaders reasonably perceived as threatening, and the rhetorical carelessness with which American policymakers treated Russian concerns all contributed to the current impasse.

These mistakes need not be repeated. The United States can acknowledge that its post-Cold War triumphalism was counterproductive without abandoning the values that animated American policy during that period. The expansion of NATO was a policy choice that can be reassessed, not a metaphysical commitment that binds future generations. The relationship between America and Russia can be reset not by demanding that Russia accept American hegemony but by recognizing that great powers must accommodation each other's legitimate interests if they are to avoid the conflicts that have historically devastated both their societies and the world.

The alliance proposed here is not a proposal for American capitulation or the abandonment of American allies. It is, rather, a proposal for the same kind of realist accommodation that has historically characterized American foreign policy at its most effective. The United States does not need Russia as a junior partner or a subordinate ally. It needs Russia as a partner in the management of global affairs whose cooperation will reduce American costs and increase American leverage in addressing the challenges that actually threaten American prosperity and security.

Addressing the Objections

Those opposed to American-Russian alliance will raise several objections that deserve serious consideration. The most significant of these concerns Russian behavior that violates American values and international norms. Russia has annexed territory in Crimea, supported separatists in eastern Ukraine, intervened in American and European elections, and pursued internal policies that suppress political opposition and civil society. These actions are genuinely objectionable, and an alliance with Russia would require that Americans accept them rather than seeking to change them through pressure and isolation.

In the case of Russia, this calculation favors alliance for several reasons. First, the leverage that comes from alliance may actually be greater than the leverage that comes from sanctions and isolation. An isolated Russia has little incentive to modify its behavior in response to American preferences; a Russia integrated into a partnership with the United States has both incentives and mechanisms for negotiation. Second, the issues on which American-Russian cooperation is possible—nuclear security, counterterrorism, energy market stability—do not require that Russia become a democracy or that Americans approve of Russian governance. They require only that both nations recognize their shared interests in these domains. The Case for US-Russia Strategic Alliance: Potential Benefits and Geopolitical Advantages

Introduction: A Hypothetical Partnership

The notion of a formal strategic alliance between the United States and the Russian Federation represents one of the most provocative scenarios in contemporary international relations. For decades, the relationship between these two nuclear superpowers has oscillated between adversarial tension and cautious cooperation, never fully transcending the legacy of Cold War mistrust. Yet the evolving global landscape—characterized by the rise of China, the fragmentation of international institutions, and the emergence of transnational challenges—has prompted some analysts to reconsider whether a strategic partnership between Washington and Moscow might serve both nations' long-term interests. This analysis examines the theoretical benefits and geopolitical advantages that could accrue to both countries from such an alliance, while acknowledging the substantial obstacles that would need to be overcome.

It is essential to recognize that this examination presents a hypothetical construct rather than a prediction or advocacy. The path toward any formal alliance faces deeply entrenched political, historical, and structural barriers. Nevertheless, exploring the potential advantages illuminates broader questions about great power dynamics, the future of international order, and the strategic calculations that underpin statecraft.

Part I: Security and Strategic Stability Benefits

Nuclear Arms Control and Strategic Equilibrium

Perhaps the most immediate and tangible benefit of a formal US-Russia alliance would be the transformation of the bilateral nuclear relationship from adversarial competition to cooperative management. Both nations currently maintain nuclear arsenals capable of inflicting civilizational devastation, and the absence of robust bilateral arms control frameworks has introduced new uncertainties into strategic stability. A formal alliance would create institutional mechanisms for deep mutual verification, coordinated nuclear doctrine, and joint responses to nuclear proliferation challenges elsewhere in the world.

The New START Treaty, which expires in 2026, represents just one example of the ad hoc approach that has characterized bilateral nuclear management. An alliance framework could institutionalize arms reduction as a permanent feature of the relationship rather than a periodic diplomatic negotiation. Furthermore, both nations share concerns about the modernization of Chinese nuclear forces and the potential for a three-way nuclear dynamic that neither country fully controls. A US-Russia alliance could provide the basis for trilateral arms control negotiations that include Beijing, addressing a vulnerability that neither superpower can manage alone.

Counterterrorism and Intelligence Cooperation

The post-September 11 era demonstrated that US-Russia intelligence cooperation, when it occurs, can yield significant security benefits. Sharing of counterterrorism information proved valuable in disrupting plots targeting both nations, and the defeat of terrorist organizations in Syria benefited from at least tacit coordination between Washington and Moscow. A formal alliance would institutionalize and expand these cooperative mechanisms, creating integrated task forces, shared databases, and real-time communication channels for addressing transnational militant threats.

Radical Islamic terrorism represents a genuine existential threat that neither nation can eliminate through unilateral action. The vast ungoverned spaces of Central Asia, the ongoing conflict in Afghanistan, and the persistence of Salafi-jihadist ideology create common vulnerabilities that both countries have a shared interest in addressing. An alliance would eliminate the bureaucratic and political barriers that currently impede effective cooperation, allowing for the pooling of analytical resources, joint operations, and coordinated public messaging.

Space Security and Missile Defense

The weaponization of space represents an emerging threat that both nations have a mutual interest in preventing. Current international legal frameworks provide inadequate mechanisms for verifying compliance with space arms control agreements, and both countries have invested heavily in counterspace capabilities. A formal alliance would create opportunities for joint development of space situational awareness systems, shared early warning networks for missile threats, and coordinated positions in international negotiations to prevent an arms race in the celestial domain.

Moreover, missile defense systems that the United States has deployed in Europe and Asia have been a persistent source of friction with Russia, which views them as potentially undermining strategic balance. An alliance framework would transform these systems from points of contention into genuine cooperative ventures, with Russia potentially participating in network architecture and receiving guarantees about system capabilities. The billions of dollars currently spent on adversarial missile defense development could instead be redirected toward integrated defensive systems that protect both nations.

Part II: Economic and Energy Cooperation Advantages

Energy Market Stabilization

Russia possesses the world's largest natural gas reserves and ranks among the top oil producers, while the United States has become a dominant force in energy markets through the shale revolution. The current relationship between these energy giants is characterized by competition, with Russian supplies to Europe competing against American LNG exports and global oil markets experiencing periodic price volatility that disadvantages both producers. A formal alliance would enable coordinated production management, joint investments in energy infrastructure, and stabilized commodity prices that benefit both economies.

The European energy market represents a particularly significant opportunity. Dependence on Russian gas has created political vulnerabilities for European nations while simultaneously generating revenue that funds Russian state activities. American LNG exports have provided an alternative that reduces European dependence but at higher prices. An alliance could facilitate the development of integrated energy systems that combine Russian production capacity with American technology and capital, creating a stable supplier-consumer relationship that eliminates the geopolitical friction currently associated with European energy imports.

Technology Transfer and Innovation

American technological leadership in areas like semiconductors, artificial intelligence, biotechnology, and quantum computing could complement Russian strengths in areas like nuclear technology, space systems, advanced materials, and certain military technologies. Current export controls and sanctions regimes severely restrict technology flows between the two nations, depriving both countries of potential innovation gains. An alliance would create frameworks for controlled technology sharing that enhances both nations' competitive positions relative to third parties, particularly China.

The semiconductor supply chain illustrates the potential benefits. American design capabilities combined with Russian material science expertise could reduce dependence on Asian manufacturing hubs that currently dominate production. Similarly, joint research and development in emerging technologies could accelerate innovation in ways that neither country could achieve independently. The elimination of technology restrictions would create new markets for American companies while providing Russia with access to capital and management expertise that could modernize its economy.

Infrastructure and Investment

Russian infrastructure needs are enormous, from transportation networks to digital telecommunications to urban development. American companies possess the capital, expertise, and management capabilities to participate in Russian infrastructure development, while Russian markets offer returns that could benefit American pension funds and institutional investors. Current sanctions regimes effectively prohibit these flows, creating opportunity costs for both economies.

The development of the Russian Arctic, in particular, requires infrastructure investments that exceed Russian domestic capital availability. Ports, railroads, energy facilities, and settlement infrastructure are all needed to exploit Arctic resources, and American participation could accelerate development while ensuring that operations meet environmental and technical standards. Similarly, Russian participation in American infrastructure projects—particularly in areas like nuclear energy and minerals processing—could provide capabilities that domestic American industry currently lacks.

Part III: Global Geopolitical Advantages

Managing the Rise of China

The emergence of China as a peer competitor represents perhaps the most significant strategic development in contemporary international relations. Both the United States and Russia face long-term challenges from Chinese economic and military expansion, though the nature of these challenges differs substantially. For the United States, Chinese power threatens the post-World War II liberal international order that has underpinned American predominance. For Russia, Chinese power creates a potentially overwhelming neighbor whose economic gravity could reduce Russia to a junior partner status in Eurasia.

A US-Russia alliance would fundamentally alter the strategic calculus by linking two of the three largest economies and military powers against a common challenge. The psychological and diplomatic impact of such a realignment would be substantial, signaling to Beijing that aggressive revisionism would face coordinated resistance. Economically, the combination of American financial markets, Russian natural resources, and combined technological capabilities would create a partnership that China could not easily match. The alliance would provide strategic depth that neither nation possesses independently while creating leverage for negotiating terms of engagement with Beijing that preserve core interests.

This is not to suggest that China would become an adversary in any simple sense—the complexities of economic interdependence make such a scenario unlikely. Rather, a US-Russia alliance would establish a framework for managing great power competition that preserves flexibility while demonstrating resolve. China would have stronger incentives to accommodate both powers' core interests if it faced a united front rather than opportunities to exploit differences.

Stability in Key Regions

Several regions of strategic importance to both nations could benefit from cooperative management under an alliance framework. In the Middle East, the United States and Russia have competing interests but also shared concerns about Iranian regional influence, political instability, and energy market management. Current competition often produces counterproductive outcomes, with arms sales fueling conflicts and rival interventions perpetuating chaos. An alliance would enable coordinated approaches to regional challenges, potentially including joint peacekeeping operations, coordinated sanctions regimes, and shared frameworks for post-conflict reconstruction.

In Central Asia, both nations have interests in preventing the emergence of terrorist sanctuaries, maintaining secular governance, and preserving independence from external domination. China currently exercises growing influence through the Belt and Road Initiative, and neither the United States nor Russia possesses sufficient leverage to balance this influence independently. An alliance would provide the basis for coordinated engagement that preserves Central Asian sovereignty while preventing any single power from achieving dominant influence.

In the Arctic, accelerating climate change is opening new shipping lanes and resource reserves that both nations have claims to managing. Current Arctic governance frameworks are inadequate for the emerging challenges, and competition among Arctic powers could produce conflicts that waste resources and degrade the environment. A US-Russia alliance would provide leadership for new governance arrangements that balance resource development with environmental protection while preserving both nations' strategic access.

Strengthening International Institutions

The post-World War II international architecture—including the United Nations, the Bretton Woods institutions, and various arms control regimes—reflects American leadership but was designed with Soviet participation as a founding member. Over time, Russian frustration with perceived marginalization in these institutions has contributed to transactional approaches that undermine international cooperation. A formal alliance would integrate Russia more deeply into the international system, providing incentives for constructive participation rather than disruptive behavior.

The United Nations Security Council represents the most obvious opportunity. Russian cooperation on issues like North Korean proliferation, Iranian nuclear ambitions, and Syrian governance has been essential but often negotiated issue-by-issue with uncertain outcomes. An alliance would create expectations of routine coordination that could dramatically enhance the Security Council's effectiveness. Similarly, Russian participation in economic institutions like the International Monetary Fund and World Bank could be expanded, providing both additional resources and voice for emerging market perspectives that currently go underrepresented.

Part IV: Domestic and Political Considerations

Economic Diversification Opportunities

Russian economic structure has long been criticized for excessive dependence on natural resource exports, a phenomenon that creates vulnerability to commodity price fluctuations and limits diversification. American partnership could accelerate diversification by providing access to capital, technology, and management expertise in manufacturing, services, and technology sectors. The elimination of sanctions would enable foreign direct investment that Russian economy desperately needs while creating markets for Russian exports beyond commodities.

For the United States, the Russian market represents an underutilized opportunity. Despite current restrictions, Russian consumer markets have demonstrated demand for American products from agriculture to automobiles to entertainment. An alliance would unlock these markets while creating jobs in American export industries. The economic benefits would be distributed across agricultural states, manufacturing regions, and technology hubs, generating political support that could sustain the alliance over time.

Scientific and Educational Exchange

The current relationship severely restricts the scientific and educational exchanges that characterized earlier periods of détente. Joint research programs, university partnerships, and student flows have all been diminished by political tensions, depriving both nations of the intellectual benefits that come from engaging talented individuals from the other society. An alliance would restore and expand these exchanges, creating networks of personal relationships that support broader cooperation.

Particularly valuable would be cooperation in areas like climate science, public health, and pandemic preparedness, where both nations face common challenges and possess complementary expertise. The COVID-19 pandemic demonstrated that biological threats respect no borders and require international cooperation for effective response. A US-Russia alliance would create frameworks for sharing epidemiological data, coordinating public health responses, and jointly developing medical countermeasures that protect both populations.

Part V: Challenges and Limitations

Historical Obstacles

Any assessment of potential US-Russia alliance must acknowledge the profound historical obstacles that would need to be overcome. By binding Russia to the West through ironclad mutual defense, economic integration, and joint stewardship of global commons, the United States can end an unwinnable cold war, relieve pressure on its overextended military, and position itself to meet the defining challenge of this century: the rise of China. From the ideological battlefields of the Cold War to the contemporary conflicts in Ukraine and Syria, Washington has largely viewed Moscow through the lens of containment and confrontation. However, the tectonic plates of global geopolitics have shifted. The unipolar moment has ended, giving way to a complex multipolar order where the greatest strategic challenges to American security and prosperity no longer emanate primarily from the Kremlin. To secure its long-term national interests, the United States must undertake a courageous and necessary realignment of its foreign policy: the pursuit of a formal strategic alliance with the Russian Federation. This is not an endorsement of any specific regime or an abandonment of democratic values, but a sober application of realist statecraft in service of American security.

The primary catalyst for this realignment is the rise of the People’s Republic of China as a peer competitor and systemic rival to the United States. For decades, American strategy has inadvertently facilitated the most dangerous geopolitical development possible: the emergence of a cohesive Sino-Russian bloc. By treating Russia as an irredeemable pariah, U.S. policy has pushed Moscow into a position of junior partnership with Beijing, providing China with the strategic depth, resource security, and diplomatic cover it needs to challenge the liberal international order. A formal U.S.-Russian alliance would shatter this alignment. Historically, the prevention of a hostile Eurasian hegemon has been the central tenet of American grand strategy, as articulated by strategists from Spykman to Brzezinski. Aligning with Russia restores the balance of power in Eurasia, denies China uncontested access to vital resources and energy, and forces Beijing to reconsider its own strategic calculus. In this context, Russia is not the enemy to be defeated, but the pivotal swing state that must be courted.

Furthermore, a strategic partnership with Russia is essential for managing existential transnational threats that respect no borders. Nuclear non-proliferation, arms control, and global strategic stability have historically relied on U.S.-Russian cooperation. As new technologies like hypersonic missiles, autonomous weapons systems, and space-based assets complicate deterrence, the absence of formal dialogue increases the risk of catastrophic miscalculation. A formal alliance structure provides the institutional framework necessary for robust verification, crisis communication, and the modernization of arms control regimes. Beyond nuclear security, the Arctic region presents a shared domain where cooperation is mandatory. As climate change opens new maritime routes and resource deposits, a collaborative U.S.-Russian framework can prevent the Arctic from becoming a militarized flashpoint and instead establish it as a zone of regulated economic and scientific partnership.

Critics will inevitably cite Russia’s internal governance and its actions in its near abroad as insurmountable obstacles to alliance. While these concerns are morally and politically significant, they must be weighed against the hierarchy of strategic threats facing the United States. Foreign policy is the art of prioritization, not perfectionism. Throughout its history, the United States has formed alliances with authoritarian regimes when doing so served vital national interests—from the Soviet Union during World War II to numerous non-democratic partners during and after the Cold War. A strategic alliance with Russia can be structured around mutual interests and verifiable commitments rather than shared values. It is a transactional, interest-based arrangement designed to manage great power competition and stabilize the international system. Moreover, engagement and integration have historically proven more effective than isolation in moderating state behavior over the long term. Total estrangement guarantees hostility; structured partnership creates off-ramps and incentives for restraint.

Finally, such a realignment would relieve the immense strain on American resources and allow for a more sustainable grand strategy. The current posture of simultaneous containment in Europe, the Middle East, and Asia stretches U.S. military, economic, and diplomatic capital to the breaking point. By converting the relationship with Russia from a liability into an asset, the United States could significantly reduce its security commitments in Europe, allowing for a right-sizing of force posture and a redirection of resources toward domestic renewal and the Indo-Pacific. This is not isolationism; it is strategic concentration. It recognizes that American power, while vast, is finite, and must be deployed where it matters most.

In conclusion, the argument for a U.S.-Russian strategic alliance is rooted not in sentiment, but in the cold logic of survival and advantage. The world has changed, and American strategy must change with it. Clinging to the animosities of the twentieth century blinds policymakers to the imperatives of the twenty-first. By embracing a formal partnership with the Russian Federation, the United States can disrupt the Sino-Russian axis, stabilize key security domains, and create the geopolitical space necessary to preserve its position and prosperity. This realignment requires political courage and intellectual honesty, but the cost of inaction—a united Eurasian bloc opposed to American interests—is a price the United States cannot afford to pay. The time has come to replace the outdated paradigm of permanent enmity with a clear-eyed strategy of interest-based alliance.

  • Economic Competition: China’s Belt and Road Initiative (BRI) is reshaping global trade dynamics. Russia, with its vast energy reserves, industrial base, and Eurasian connections, could serve as a counterweight to China’s economic dominance, particularly in Europe and Central Asia.
  • Technological and Cyber Warfare: Both the U.S. and Russia face severe threats from China’s cyber capabilities and AI-driven military advancements. A formal alliance would allow for joint defense research, intelligence sharing, and cybersecurity cooperation, strengthening both nations against Chinese digital dominance.

Without Russia as a partner, the U.S. is fighting a two-front war—against both China and Russia—while China benefits from a divided West. An alliance would force China to confront a united front, making it far less likely to pursue reckless aggression.

2. Nuclear Deterrence and Global Stability

The U.S. and Russia remain the world’s two largest nuclear powers, each possessing thousands of warheads. The risk of nuclear escalation, whether by accident, miscalculation, or rogue actors, is higher than at any point since the Cuban Missile Crisis. A formal alliance would:

  • Economic Self-Sabotage: Our sanctions have hurt our own farmers, our own energy sector, our own workers—while China laughs all the way to the bank, buying up Russian oil, gas, and technology at a discount.

Why Russia? Why Now?

Some will ask: "Why Russia? Why not just focus on China?" The answer is simple: Because we cannot defeat China alone. And because Russia is not our enemy—China is.

  • A Shared Enemy: China is the greatest threat to American security in the 21st century. It seeks to dominate the Indo-Pacific, undermine our alliances, and replace the dollar with the yuan. Russia understands this. They have fought proxy wars against Chinese expansionism in Central Asia. They have warned us about China’s ambitions. And yet, we push them into Beijing’s arms with every new sanction, every new NATO expansion.
  • Nuclear Realism: The world is one miscalculation away from Armageddon. Russia and the U.S. hold 90% of the world’s nuclear arsenals. If we do not de-escalate, negotiate, and build trust, we risk accidental war—not because of Russian aggression, but because of miscommunication, brinkmanship, and the folly of those who believe nuclear war can be "won."
  • Energy and Economic Independence: America is the world’s top energy producer, yet we beg the Saudis and beg the world for oil while Russia sits on the largest natural gas reserves on Earth. A New Entente: The Case for a US-Russia Strategic Alliance

Rethinking the Post-Cold War Orthodoxy

For three decades, American foreign policy has rested on a foundational assumption: that the United States and Russia are destined to be rivals, at best managed competitors, and at worst adversaries locked in a zero-sum contest for influence in Europe, Eurasia, and the developing world. This assumption, inherited from the triumphant moment of 1991 and calcified by the NATO expansion debates, the color revolutions, the wars in Georgia and Ukraine, and the strategic drift of the past twenty years, has produced a costly and counterproductive status quo. It is time to discard it.

The United States should pursue a formal strategic alliance with the Russian Federation. This is not a naïve call for trust where none exists, nor a naive embrace of an authoritarian system. It is a hardheaded recognition that two of the world's three largest nuclear powers, two of its most consequential energy producers, and two of its most militarily capable states cannot afford the perpetual friction that defines their current relationship. The risks of the present trajectory—escalation in Ukraine, confrontation in Syria, dangerous incidents at sea and in the air, an uncontrolled arms race, and the steady erosion of the last remnants of strategic stability—are simply too high. A serious reorientation toward partnership is the only responsible course.

The Imperative of Nuclear Stewardship

The single most compelling reason for a US-Russia alliance is the most obvious: together, the two countries hold approximately 90 percent of the world's nuclear weapons. The doctrines of both nations envision scenarios in which these weapons could be used, and both maintain hair-trigger alert postures that have repeatedly brought the world to the edge of catastrophe. The Cuban Missile Crisis, the 1983 NATO Able Archer exercise, the 1995 Norwegian rocket incident, and numerous other close calls demonstrate that the existing deterrence relationship is sustainable only through constant, careful management—and that even careful management is not always sufficient.

Alliances between nuclear powers have a stabilizing effect beyond what mere arms control agreements can achieve. The deep intelligence sharing, communication channels, joint planning, and political trust that characterize formal alliances reduce the probability of miscalculation far more effectively than the ad hoc, often-strained mechanisms that currently connect Washington and Moscow. The New START Treaty is valuable, but it is a passive constraint; an alliance would be an active, living framework for managing nuclear risks. This alone justifies the effort.

The China Factor

For decades, American strategists have treated Russia as the primary long-term geopolitical challenge in Eurasia, while treating China primarily through the lens of economic engagement. This categorization no longer reflects reality. China is now the United States' principal peer competitor in military, technological, and economic terms, and it is a competitor that presents a far more formidable long-term challenge than a declining, demographically troubled Russia with a GDP smaller than Italy's.

Moscow, for its part, has come to view Beijing with growing unease. The "no limits" partnership announced in 2022 obscures the reality that Russia is increasingly the junior partner in its relationship with China, dependent on Chinese demand for its commodities and increasingly drawn into serving Chinese strategic interests in Central Asia, the Arctic, and beyond. A strategic alignment with Washington offers Russia an off-ramp from this dependency. For the United States, even a partial decoupling of Russia from China would be a strategic windfall—dividing what is currently a loose anti-Western alignment and complicating Beijing's strategic planning.

The realist insight that one's adversary's adversary is a potential partner remains as valid today as it was for Kissinger in 1972. A US-Russia alignment would not be a love match, but it is entirely consistent with balance-of-power logic that has guided great power statecraft for centuries.

Ending the Periphery Wars

The frozen and active conflicts in which the United States and Russia find themselves on opposing sides—Ukraine, Syria, Libya, and various African theaters—are not producing outcomes favorable to American interests. They are consuming resources, generating humanitarian catastrophes, creating fertile ground for terrorism, and providing fodder for domestic political manipulation in both countries. An alliance framework would permit the diplomatic off-ramps that the current adversarial relationship renders impossible.

In Ukraine specifically, the status quo is unsustainable. A security architecture that includes Russia, rather than one designed to exclude it, offers the only realistic path to a settlement that respects the legitimate security concerns of all parties. In Syria, a coordinated approach to the residual ISIS threat, to refugee flows, and to the political settlement is far more likely to succeed than the current arrangement of mutual obstruction. A US-Russia alliance would not magically resolve these disputes, but it would transform the diplomatic environment in which they are addressed from one of suspicion to one of common purpose.

Energy, Climate, and the Arctic

Russia possesses the world's largest natural gas reserves, substantial oil reserves, and enormous potential in nuclear energy, hydrogen, and critical minerals. The energy transition that the United States and its partners are pursuing will be vastly more difficult and expensive without Russian cooperation. A strategic alliance would unlock joint ventures in Arctic development, in critical mineral supply chains (where Russia is rich in nickel, palladium, rare earths, and other materials essential to clean energy technology), and in the development of next-generation energy systems.

The Arctic is opening at a pace that exceeds most projections, and the region is becoming a theater of intensifying competition. Cooperative governance, joint scientific research, and coordinated infrastructure investment—none of which are possible under the current relationship—would serve both nations' interests and the interests of the broader international community.

A Realistic Acknowledgment of Differences

Advocating for alliance is not the same as advocating for the abandonment of American values or interests. The United States will continue to have profound disagreements with Russia over domestic governance, human rights, the treatment of civil society, and the architecture of the international order. An alliance does not require pretending these differences do not exist. It requires recognizing that great powers have always managed profound ideological differences when their strategic interests aligned—from the US-China rapprochement of the 1970s, to the Reagan-Thatcher relationship with Deng Xiaoping's China, to the long Anglo-American "special relationship" sustained across vast cultural and political divergences.

Indeed, an alliance creates channels through which American concerns about Russian domestic policy can be raised more effectively, not less. Adversaries do not persuade each other; partners do.

The Costs of Inaction

The alternative to a strategic realignment is more of the same: a slow drift toward confrontation, punctuated by crises that bring the two countries close to direct military conflict. Sanctions have failed to alter Russian behavior in any of the ways their architects intended; they have instead pushed Russia closer to China and Iran, accelerated the development of alternative payment systems, and inflicted significant collateral damage on the European economies the United States claims to protect. NATO expansion has not produced security for Eastern Europe; it has produced the very conflict it was meant to prevent. Arms control has collapsed. Diplomatic relationships are at their lowest point in decades.

This trajectory is not sustainable, and it is not inevitable. The same human ingenuity that produced the structures of the post-Cold War order can produce new ones. A US-Russia strategic alliance is ambitious, certainly, and it would require courage from leaders in both countries who have built careers on the rhetoric of rivalry. But the alternative—a world in which two nuclear superpowers stumble from crisis to crisis, with an ascendant China benefiting from their division—is a far more dangerous and far more likely future than the alliance that prudence demands.

Conclusion: A Vision Worth Pursuing

The United States stands at an inflection point. The unipolar moment has ended. The question is not whether the international system will be reorganized, but on what terms. A strategic alliance with Russia offers the prospect of a more stable, more prosperous, and less dangerous reorganization—one in which the two great nuclear powers become stewards of a common global order rather than protagonists in a new cold war. This is a vision worthy of American statecraft at its best: ambitious, realistic, and grounded in a clear-eyed assessment of national interest. The time to pursue it is now.

Some strategists (notably some realists) have argued:

  • A US–Russia entente could prevent a bipolar world dominated by a single peer competitor.
  • Combined leverage on issues like Taiwan, trade practices, and South China Sea militarization would be substantial.
  • It would limit Beijing's ability to drive wedges between Western powers.

4. Economic and Energy Cooperation

  • Energy Markets: Coordinated rather than competing energy exports to Europe and Asia could stabilize global prices and reduce the weaponization of energy supply.
  • Arctic Development: Joint governance of Arctic shipping routes, resource extraction, and environmental protection would benefit both nations with Arctic coastlines.
  • Sanctions Relief: Formal rapprochement could unlock trade, technology transfer, and investment opportunities currently blocked.
  • Scientific Collaboration: Joint research in physics, medicine, and space (building on the ISS legacy) would advance both nations' capabilities.

5. Multilateral Institutional Reform

  • UN Security Council: Both as permanent members, cooperation could unblock action on crises that currently deadlock the body.
  • International Order: Joint leadership could reform institutions (IMF, World Bank, WHO) to reflect 21st-century realities more effectively.
  • Conflict Resolution: Coordinated mediation in regional disputes (Libya, Yemen, Ukraine, Caucasus) could replace great-power rivalry with shared problem-solving.

6. European Security Architecture

  • A new framework (e.g., replacing or reforming NATO-Russia tensions) could reduce military spending across the continent.
  • Resolution of conflicts in Ukraine, Moldova, and the Caucasus would free resources for development.
  • Conventional forces agreements (similar to the 1990 CFE Treaty) would create predictability.

7. Emerging Domain Cooperation

  • Cybersecurity: Joint norms against critical infrastructure attacks, election interference, and ransomware could establish global standards.
  • Space: Coordinated rules against weaponization of space, debris management, and shared satellite services.
  • AI Governance: Bilateral leadership on regulating military AI, autonomous weapons, and frontier technologies.

8. Global Public Goods

  • Climate Change: Russia is a major emitter; cooperation on methane reduction, carbon markets, and Arctic preservation would advance global goals.
  • Pandemic Preparedness: Joint disease surveillance and vaccine cooperation (as partially seen with COVID-19 efforts).
  • Maritime Security: Anti-piracy, freedom of navigation, and shipping lane protection.

9. Domestic Political Benefits

  • Leaders on both sides could redirect defense spending toward domestic priorities: infrastructure, education, healthcare.
  • Reduced external threat perception often correlates with civil liberties and democratic norms at home.
  • Economic integration tends to expand middle-class prosperity.

10. Historical Precedents

Notable periods of cooperation suggest such alignment is feasible:

  • WWII Alliance (1941–1945): The "Grand Alliance" defeated fascism through extraordinary coordination.
  • Early Post-Cold War (1991–1993): The Nunn-Lugar Cooperative Threat Reduction program dismantled thousands of Soviet nuclear weapons.
  • Iran Nuclear Deal (2015): The JCPOA demonstrated that alignment on specific issues is achievable.

Important Caveats

Any serious analysis must acknowledge the significant obstacles to such an alliance:

  • Deeply divergent political systems and values
  • Ongoing conflict in Ukraine since 2014 (escalated in 2022)
  • Mutual public distrust built over decades
  • Competing interests in the post-Soviet space
  • Alliance structures (NATO, CSTO) that create institutional barriers

Analysts typically frame US–Russia relations as ranging from cooperative engagement to managed competition—formal alliance sits at the optimistic end of the spectrum and would require resolution of major conflicts, regime changes, or fundamental shifts in threat perception.

My fellow Americans,

The case for partnership is not naïve. It is urgent.

First, the security of our children. We possess, together, the overwhelming majority of the world's nuclear weapons. The Cold War taught us that brinksmanship ends in ash. Second, the prosperity of our workers. Russian energy, American technology, Russian rare earth minerals, American agricultural abundance — these are not threats. They are opportunities. Sanctions and tariffs have cost American farmers markets, cost American manufacturers inputs, cost American consumers at the pump. A partnership opens trade, investment, and joint development that could power the next industrial revolution — and do it in both our countries.

Third, the great challenges that will define this century. Pandemics. Climate change. Cybersecurity. The exploration of the cosmos. The governance of artificial intelligence. Do we believe these problems are solved by the United States acting alone? Or by Russia? Neither. They are solved by the great powers working together, or they are not solved at all. An alliance with Russia multiplies American power; isolation divides it.

Fourth, the silenced voices of peace. There are millions of Russians and millions of Americans who want exactly what we want — safe neighborhoods, opportunities for their children, dignity in old age. The war profiteers, the defense contractors, the ideological hardliners in both capitals — they thrive on enmity. They will say our allies in Europe would object. Our allies want security. A world in which the two largest nuclear powers are partners is a safer Europe, not a more threatened one.

Let us imagine the alternative. Another decade of proxy wars, of frozen conflicts, of diplomats expelled, of treaties torn up. Another trillion dollars spent on weapons while our bridges crumble and our students are forgotten. Another generation taught to see a child in Moscow as an enemy rather than a fellow dreamer.

That is not the American character.

The American character is the character of FDR, who reached out to a Soviet ally when the world burned. It is the character of Kennedy, who dreamed of going to the moon together. It is the character of Reagan, who looked Gorbachev in the eye and chose the possibility of peace. Our greatest leaders have always understood that real strength is the courage to build something new with those we once called foes.
